literal: Geography Treatise, Part 1
idiomatic: Geography Treatise I

literal: Emperor Yao divided the realm into Nine Provinces.
idiomatic: Yao divided the world into the Nine Provinces.

literal: Shun, because Ji and Qing were large, split off You, Bing, and Ying, making twelve provinces.
idiomatic: Shun carved You, Bing, and Ying from the oversized Ji and Qing domains, yielding twelve provinces.

literal: You lay between Bo and Jie; north of Bing were Dai and Shuo; Ying reached east to the Liao Sea.
idiomatic: You province lay between the Bo and Jie seas; Bing had Dai and Shuo to its north; Ying extended east to the Liao Sea.

literal: Its land backed mountains and girded sea; its people took up weapons, roused martial guard; wind and temper were firm and strong—from antiquity a land where armies were deployed.
idiomatic: The region backed mountains and faced the sea; its people took up arms and stood on martial guard; the local temper was hard and bold—a classic military frontier since antiquity.

literal: Taizu, with the masses of the Dieci tribe, replaced the Yaolian clan, rose at Linhuang, and built the imperial capital;
idiomatic: Taizu, leading the Dieci tribe, supplanted the Yaolian house, raised his seat at Linhuang, and founded the imperial capital;

literal: east he annexed Bohai and gained one hundred three walled settlements.
idiomatic: to the east he absorbed Bohai and seized one hundred and three walled towns.

literal: Taizong established Jin and held the sixteen prefectures You, Zhuo, Tan, Ji, Shun, Ying, Ping, Yu, Shuo, Yun, Ying, Xin, Gui, Ru, Wu, and Huan—thus cutting the old You, Bing, and Ying tracts and straddling them.
idiomatic: When Taizong secured Jin he took sixteen prefectures—You, Zhuo, Tan, Ji, Shun, Ying, Ping, Yu, Shuo, Yun, Ying, Xin, Gui, Ru, Wu, and Huan—so the state spanned the ancient You, Bing, and Ying heartland.

literal: East he faced Goryeo; west he made the Xia state a vassal; south he treated Later Jin as a son and Song as a brother; Wuyue and Southern Tang sent tribute by sea.
idiomatic: To the east lay Goryeo; to the west the Xia acknowledged subjection; to the south Later Jin was treated as a son-state and Song as a brother; Wuyue and Southern Tang paid tribute by sea.

literal: Alas, how grand it was!
idiomatic: How vast its sway had become!

literal: The Liao state was formerly called Khitan, originally Xianbei land, dwelling in the Liao marshes—1,130 li from Yugu Pass and another 714 li from Youzhou.
idiomatic: Liao's forebears were the Khitan, a Xianbei people living in the Liao marshes—1,130 li from Yugu Pass and 714 li farther from Youzhou.

literal: South it controlled Huanglong; north it belted the Huang River; Lengling screened the right; the Liao River trench lay to the left.
idiomatic: To the south it held Huanglong; to the north ran the Huang River; Cold Ridge guarded the west; the Liao River ditch lay on the east.

literal: The highlands had many elms and willows; the low wetlands abounded in reeds and rushes.
idiomatic: Uplands bore elm and willow; marshy flats were rich in reed and rush.

literal: In Northern Wei times its territory ran several hundred li.
idiomatic: Under the Northern Wei its domain covered several hundred li.

literal: By Tang the Dahe clan nibbled away the lands of Fuyu, Shiwei, Xi, and Mohe until the region reached more than two thousand li.
idiomatic: By Tang the Dahe clan had eaten into Fuyu, Shiwei, Xi, and Mohe territory until their lands exceeded two thousand li.

literal: In the third year of Zhenguan their land was made Xuan Prefecture.
idiomatic: In Zhenguan year 3 the court created Xuan Prefecture on their soil.

literal: Soon Songmo Protectorate was set up, the eight divisions made into prefectures, each with a cishi: the Daji division as Qiaoluo Prefecture, the Hebian as Danhan, the Duhuo as Wufeng, the Fena as Yuling, the Tubian as Rilian, the Ruixi as Tuhe, the Zhuijin as Wandan, the Fu as Pili and Chishan two prefectures.
idiomatic: Songmo Protectorate followed, with eight tribal divisions converted to prefectures, each with a prefect: Daji became Qiaoluo; Hebian became Danhan; Duhuo, Wufeng; Fena, Yuling; Tubian, Rilian; Ruixi, Tuhe; Zhuijin, Wandan; Fu, the twin prefectures Pili and Chishan.

literal: The Dahe Kuge was made commissioner with credentials over the ten prefectures' military affairs.
idiomatic: Dahe Kuge received credentials as commissioner for military affairs across the ten prefectures.

literal: Dividing prefectures and establishing officials began in this fashion.
idiomatic: Prefecture divisions and official posts took their start here.

literal: By the Five Dynasties they opened land three thousand li east and west.
idiomatic: By the Five Dynasties their domain stretched three thousand li from east to west.

literal: The Yaolian clan renamed the eight divisions Zhilejie, Yishihuo, Shihuo, Nawei, Pinmei, Neihuiji, Jijie, and Xiwu divisions, with forty-one subordinate counties.
idiomatic: The Yaolian house retitled the eight divisions Zhilejie, Yishihuo, Shihuo, Nawei, Pinmei, Neihuiji, Jijie, and Xiwu, governing forty-one counties beneath them.

literal: Each division had a cishi; counties had magistrates.
idiomatic: Each division received a prefect; each county a magistrate.

literal: Taizong made the imperial capital Shangjing, raised Youzhou to Nanjing, renamed Nanjing to Dongjing, Shengzong walled Zhongjing, Xingzong raised Yunzhou to Xijing—thus the Five Capitals were complete.
idiomatic: Taizong made the imperial seat Shangjing, elevated Youzhou to Nanjing, later renamed it Dongjing; Shengzong built Zhongjing; Xingzong raised Yunzhou to Xijing—completing the Five Capitals.

literal: They also built prefectures at strategic points with captives from campaigns, often keeping old settlement names;
idiomatic: Campaign captives also seeded prefectures at strategic nodes, often under their former place names;

literal: private slaves were added to establish subordinate-domain prefectures.
idiomatic: private slaves were settled to form subordinate-domain prefectures.

literal: In all: five capitals, six prefectures, one hundred fifty-six prefectures, armies, and walled towns, two hundred nine counties, fifty-two tribal divisions, and sixty subject states.
idiomatic: In total there were five capitals, six superior prefectures, 156 prefectures, armies, and fortified towns, 209 counties, 52 tribal divisions, and 60 subject states.

literal: East to the sea, west to the Golden Mountains and on to the shifting sands, north to the Luchiju River, south to the White Ditch—ten thousand li in extent.
idiomatic: Its bounds ran east to the sea, west to the Golden Mountains and the shifting sands, north to the Luchiju River, and south to the White Ditch—a domain of ten thousand li.

literal: ○ Upper Capital Circuit
idiomatic: ○ Shangjing Circuit

literal: Shangjing Linhuang Prefecture was originally Han Liaodong commandery's Xi'anping land.
idiomatic: Shangjing's Linhuang Prefecture occupied the old Han Liaodong commandery seat of Xi'anping.

literal: Xin Mang called it Beianping.
idiomatic: Xin Mang renamed the place Beianping.

literal: Taizu took the momentum of Tianti, Mengguo, and Bielu three mountains in the reed marsh, shot a gold-tipped arrow to mark it, and called it Longmei Palace.
idiomatic: Taizu seized the heights of Tianti, Mengguo, and Bielu among the reed marshes, marked the site with a gold-notched arrow, and named it Longmei Palace.

literal: In the third year of Shence a city was built, named Huangdu.
idiomatic: In Shence year 3 he walled a city there and called it Huangdu.

literal: In the thirteenth year of Tianxian it was renamed Shangjing; the prefecture was called Linhuang.
idiomatic: In Tianxian year 13 the seat became Shangjing and the prefecture Linhuang.

literal: The Lailiu River flowed from the northwest southward, encircled the capital on three sides, and entered the Qu River to the east; to the north and east it became the Anchu River.
idiomatic: The Lailiu River ran from the northwest, wrapped the capital on three sides, and entered the Qu River eastward; north and east of the city it formed the Anchu River.

literal: There were also the Imperial River, Sha River, Hei River, Huang River, Yazi River, Talu River, Lang River, Canger River, Wangzi River, Luchiju River, Yinyang River, Zhu River, Yuanyang Lake, Xingguo Huimin Lake, Guangji Lake, salt marshes, Baigou Marsh, Huoshen Shoal, Mayu Mountain, Tu'er Mountain, Yaque Mountain, Salt Mountain, Zao Mountain, Song Mountain, Pingdi Pine Forest, Dafu Mountain, Lie Mountain, Qulie Mountain, Lede Mountain—where Tang had enfeoffed the Dahe Lede King and a tomb still stood.
idiomatic: Waters and landmarks included the Imperial, Sha, Hei, Huang, Yazi, Talu, Lang, Canger, and Wangzi rivers; the Luchiju and Yinyang rivers; Zhu River; Yuanyang, Xingguo Huimin, and Guangji lakes; salt marshes; Baigou Marsh; Huoshen Shoal; Mayu, Tu'er, Yaque, Salt, Zao, and Song mountains; the Pingdi pine belt; Dafu, Lie, Qulie, and Lede peaks—the last holding the tomb of the Dahe Lede King enfeoffed by Tang.

literal: Households 36,500; it governed twenty-five armies, prefectures, and walled towns and ruled ten counties.
idiomatic: It registered 36,500 households, governed twenty-five armies, prefectures, and fortified towns, and administered ten counties.

literal: Linhuang County.
idiomatic: County seat: Linhuang.

literal: At the start of Tianzan Taizu attacked south into Yan and Ji and scattered captured households along the north bank of the Huang River; the county faced the Huang River and took its name.
idiomatic: Early in Tianzan Taizu raided Yan and Ji and settled captives along the Huang River's north bank; the county sat on that river and was named for it.

literal: The soil suited planting.
idiomatic: The land was good for crops.

literal: Households 3,500.
idiomatic: 3,500 households.

literal: Changtai County.
idiomatic: County seat: Changtai.

literal: Originally people of Bohai's Changping County; Taizu, attacking Da Yinzhen, first took this settlement and moved its people northwest of the capital to live mixed with Han.
idiomatic: Its settlers came from Bohai's Changping County; when Taizu attacked Da Yinzhen he seized this town first and resettled its people northwest of the capital among Han households.

literal: Households 4,000.
idiomatic: 4,000 households.

literal: Dingba County.
idiomatic: Dingba County.

literal: Originally people of Fuyu prefecture's Qiangshi County; Taizu took Fuyu and moved them west of the capital to live mixed with Han, allotting land to farm.
idiomatic: They were originally from Fuyu prefecture's Qiangshi County; after Taizu conquered Fuyu he resettled them west of the capital among Han farmers on divided fields.

literal: In the eighth year of Tonghe, households of the various palace supervisory offices were used to establish it.
idiomatic: Tonghe year 8 brought settlers drawn from palace supervisory offices to found the county.

literal: It was subordinate to Changning Palace.
idiomatic: It fell under Changning Palace.

literal: Households 2,000.
idiomatic: 2,000 households.

literal: Baohe County.
idiomatic: Baohe County.

literal: Originally people of Bohai's Fuli County; Taizu took Longzhou and moved all Fuli people scattered south of the capital.
idiomatic: Its people came from Bohai's Fuli County; when Taizu seized Longzhou he dispersed Fuli households south of the capital.

literal: In the eighth year of Tonghe, households of the various palace supervisory offices were used to establish it.
idiomatic: Tonghe year 8 used households from palace supervisory offices to establish the county.

literal: It was subordinate to Zhangmin Palace.
idiomatic: It belonged to Zhangmin Palace.

literal: Households 4,000.
idiomatic: 4,000 households.

literal: Lu County.
idiomatic: Lu County.

literal: Originally people of Youzhou's Lu County; in the first year of Tianzan Taizu took Ji Prefecture and carried off Lu County people, placing them east of the capital mixed with Bohai.
idiomatic: They were originally from Youzhou's Lu County; in Tianzan year 1 Taizu captured Ji Prefecture, seized Lu households, and settled them east of the capital among Bohai people.

literal: It was subordinate to Chongde Palace.
idiomatic: It was attached to Chongde Palace.

literal: Households 3,000.
idiomatic: 3,000 households.

literal: Yisu County.
idiomatic: Yisu County.

literal: Originally people of Liaodong and Bohai; in the ninth year of Taiping, Da Yanlin stirred the Liaodong Yi to rebel, besieged for a year, then surrendered; all were moved north of the capital and a county was set to house them.
idiomatic: Its founders were Liaodong and Bohai people; in Taiping year 9 Da Yanlin roused Liaodong tribes to revolt, held out a year, then submitted; the court moved them north of the capital and founded a county for them.

literal: That year families of Bohai rebels were also moved and placed there.
idiomatic: The same year households of Bohai rebels were relocated there as well.

literal: Households 1,000.
idiomatic: 1,000 households.

literal: Qianliao County.
idiomatic: County seat: Qianliao.

literal: Originally Bohai people of Liaodong counties; when Da Yanlin rebelled, the boldest plotters were chosen and placed at the ruler's side.
idiomatic: Originally Bohai from Liaodong counties; during Da Yanlin's revolt the boldest conspirators were kept at court.

literal: Later when the city surrendered they were executed; their families were moved northeast of the capital, hence the name.
idiomatic: When the city later surrendered they were executed and their families resettled northeast of the capital—hence the name.

literal: Households 1,000.
idiomatic: 1,000 households.

literal: Bohai County.
idiomatic: Bohai County.

literal: Originally people of Dongjing; because of rebellion they were moved and settled.
idiomatic: Originally Dongjing people, relocated here after a rebellion.

literal: Xingren County.
idiomatic: Xingren County.

literal: Established in the second year of Kaitai.
idiomatic: Founded in Kaitai year 2.

literal: Xuanhua County.
idiomatic: Xuanhua County.

literal: Originally people of Liaodong's Shenhua County; Taizu took Yalu Prefecture and moved all its people south of the capital.
idiomatic: They came from Liaodong's Shenhua County; when Taizu seized Yalu Prefecture he moved the entire population south of the capital.

literal: In the eighth year of Tonghe, households of the various palace supervisory offices were used to establish it.
idiomatic: Tonghe year 8 settled households from palace supervisory offices to establish the county.

literal: It was subordinate to Zhangmin Palace.
idiomatic: It belonged to Zhangmin Palace.

literal: Households 4,000.
idiomatic: 4,000 households.

literal: Shangjing was the place of Taizu's founding enterprise.
idiomatic: Shangjing was Taizu's founding seat.

literal: Backed by mountains and embracing the sea, heaven's barriers could secure it.
idiomatic: Mountains guarded it and the sea lay before it—natural defenses enough to hold firm.

literal: The land was fertile for planting; grass and water favored herding.
idiomatic: Soil was rich for farming; pasture and water favored livestock.

literal: One gold-notched arrow—a foundation of two hundred years—how stout!
idiomatic: A single gold-notched arrow laid a foundation two centuries long—how solid it stood.

literal: In the first year of Tianxian, after pacifying Bohai and returning, the outer walls were extended, palaces built, and the name taken from Tianzan.
idiomatic: In Tianxian year 1, after Bohai was pacified, the outer ramparts were expanded, palaces erected, and the complex named for Tianzan.

literal: Three great halls were raised: called Kaihuang, Ande, and Wuluan.
idiomatic: Three great halls went up: Kaihuang, Ande, and Wuluan.

literal: Within were portraits of emperors through the ages; on each new and full moon, festival day, and memorial day, civil and military officials of Dongjing all came to offer sacrifice.
idiomatic: Inside hung portraits of emperors through the ages; on new and full moons, festivals, and memorial days civil and military officials from Dongjing all came to sacrifice.

literal: In the inner city's southeast corner Tianxiong Temple was built to enshrine the portrait of the late father, Emperor Xuanjian.
idiomatic: At the inner city's southeast corner Tianxiong Temple housed the image of the late Emperor Xuanjian.

literal: That year Taizu died; Empress Yingtian at Yijie Temple severed her wrist and placed Taizu's tomb.
idiomatic: That year Taizu died; at Yijie Temple Empress Yingtian cut off her wrist and established Taizu's tomb.

literal: The Severed-Wrist Tower was built at the temple and a stele erected.
idiomatic: A Severed-Wrist Tower was raised at the temple with a commemorative stele.

literal: Taizong, supporting Jin, sent Chancellor Feng Dao, Liu Xu, and others with credentials, full guard of honor, and court robes here to invest Taizong and Empress Yingtian with honorific titles.
idiomatic: When Taizong backed Jin he sent Feng Dao, Liu Xu, and others bearing credentials, full honors, and court robes to invest Taizong and Empress Yingtian.

literal: Taizong ordered the tribal ministries to follow Han ritual; he entered Kaihuang Hall, opened Chengtian Gate to receive rites, and therefore changed Huangdu to Shangjing.
idiomatic: Taizong commanded tribal ministries to follow Han ceremony, entered Kaihuang Hall, opened Chengtian Gate for the investiture, and renamed Huangdu Shangjing.

literal: The wall was two zhang high, without watch-towers; the circuit measured twenty-seven li.
idiomatic: Walls stood two zhang high without watch-towers; the circuit ran twenty-seven li.

literal: Gates: east called Yingchun and Yan'er;
idiomatic: Eastern gates: Yingchun and Yan'er;

literal: south called Shunyang;
idiomatic: south: Shunyang;

literal: called Nanfu;
idiomatic: and Nanfu;

literal: west called Jinfeng and Xiyan'er.
idiomatic: west: Jinfeng and Xiyan'er.

literal: The north was called the Imperial City, three zhang high, with towers and parapets.
idiomatic: The northern quarter was the Imperial City—three zhang high with towers and parapets.

literal: Gates: east Andong, south Dashun, west Qiande, north Gongchen.
idiomatic: Its gates were Andong east, Dashun south, Qiande west, and Gongchen north.

literal: Within was the Great Inner.
idiomatic: Inside stood the Great Inner.

literal: The inner south gate was Chengtian, with tower-pavilions;
idiomatic: The inner south gate Chengtian had tower-pavilions;

literal: east gate Donghua, west Xihua.
idiomatic: east gate Donghua, west gate Xihua.

literal: These were the passages in and out of the inner precinct.
idiomatic: These were the inner precinct's main passages.

literal: East along the central south avenue: the garrison commissioner's office, next the Salt and Iron Gate, next the south gate, Longsi Street.
idiomatic: Along the main south avenue eastward stood the garrison commissioner's office, then the Salt and Iron Gate, then the south gate and Longsi Street.

literal: South was Linhuang Prefecture; beside it Linhuang County.
idiomatic: To the south lay Linhuang Prefecture with Linhuang County beside it.

literal: Southwest of the county was Chongxiao Temple, built by Empress Chengtian.
idiomatic: Southwest of the county stood Chongxiao Temple, founded by Empress Chengtian.
